details:
**Midnight's Children**
Rushdie's 1981 novel, which won the Booker Prize, written while he was working as an advertising copywriter. It follows the 1,001 "midnight's children" born during the first hour of August 15, 1947, the moment India became independent and was partitioned from Pakistan, each of whom has a magical power. It is the most common title clue and giveaway.

**Saleem Sinai**
The narrator of Midnight's Children, born at the exact stroke of midnight on independence day and raised by a wealthy family in Bombay. His huge, constantly dripping nose gives him telepathy, which he uses to gather the other children into the Midnight's Children's Conference. He later marries Parvati-the-witch, and he loses his telepathy after sinus surgery.

**Mary Pereira and Shiva**
Mary Pereira, a midwife, switches two newborns at birth, so Saleem grows up rich while the real heir is raised as the son of the poor accordion player Wee Willie Winkie. That other child, "Shiva-of-the-knees," has deadly powerful knees and becomes Saleem's rival and the novel's antagonist. Mary later works at the Braganza Pickle Factory and eventually confesses the swap.

**Aadam Aziz and the perforated sheet**
Saleem's grandfather, a doctor, falls in love with his future wife Naseem by examining her one part at a time through a hole in a sheet held up by her family. This opening episode of Midnight's Children is a recurring early clue.

**Other Midnight's Children details**
Saleem's sister becomes a famous singer and is nicknamed the Brass Monkey. Saleem is hit on the head by a silver spittoon, loses his memory, and wanders in the Sundarbans jungle. Indira Gandhi appears as "the Widow," the Englishman William Methwold sells villas to Saleem's family, and one chapter is titled "Snakes and Ladders."

**The Satanic Verses**
Rushdie's 1988 novel, whose title refers to verses supposedly praising three pagan goddesses that were briefly included in revelations and then withdrawn. Dream sequences show a prophet called Mahound in the city of Jahilia, with characters such as the priestess Hind and the satirist Baal. Many Muslims considered it blasphemous, and it led directly to the fatwa against Rushdie.

**Gibreel Farishta and Saladin Chamcha**
The two Indian actors who open The Satanic Verses by falling from a hijacked plane that explodes over the English Channel, and surviving. Gibreel comes to believe he is the archangel Gabriel, while Saladin, a voice actor fired from the children's show The Aliens Show, turns into a horned, goatlike devil. Out of revenge, Saladin uses his talent for voices in obscene phone calls that make Gibreel jealous of his lover, the Everest climber Alleluia "Allie" Cone. Gibreel later kills Allie and then himself.

**Ayesha's pilgrimage to the Arabian Sea**
A dream sequence in The Satanic Verses in which Ayesha, a girl covered in butterflies who claims to receive messages from the archangel Gibreel, leads her villagers on a pilgrimage to Mecca. She convinces them the Arabian Sea will part for them, and they walk into the water and drown.

**The fatwa**
In 1989 Iran's Ayatollah Khomeini issued a fatwa calling for Rushdie's death over The Satanic Verses, forcing him into hiding. The novel's Japanese translator, Hitoshi Igarashi, was stabbed to death in 1991, and Rushdie himself was stabbed in 2022 before giving a public lecture. He describes his years in hiding in the memoir Joseph Anton (2012), titled after the alias he used.

**Haroun and the Sea of Stories**
Rushdie's 1990 children's novel, which opens in "the saddest of cities." Haroun's father Rashid, a storyteller nicknamed "the Shah of Blah," loses his gift of storytelling. They travel to the Valley of K and then to the moon Kahani, where Haroun meets Iff the Water Genie and Butt the Hoopoe and the kingdoms of Gup and Chup are at war.

**The Ground Beneath Her Feet**
A 1999 novel that retells the Orpheus and Eurydice myth through the world of rock music. Ormus Cama, a member of the band VTO, writes the title song for his love, the singer Vina Apsara; U2 later set lyrics from the novel to music as a real song.

**The Moor's Last Sigh**
A 1995 novel narrated by Moraes "Moor" Zogoiby, who ages twice as fast as normal. Its title refers to the legendary sigh of Boabdil, the last Muslim ruler of Granada, as he surrendered the city. Moraes ends up held captive in a Spanish replica of the Alhambra.

**Shame**
A 1983 novel set in a country resembling Pakistan. Omar Khayyam Shakil is raised in the border town of Q by three sisters, Chhunni, Munnee, and Bunny, who all pretend to have given birth to him, and he witnesses the rivalry of Iskandar Harappa and Raza Hyder. Raza's wife Bilquis has a daughter nicknamed Good News.

**Grimus**
Rushdie's first novel (1975). Its protagonist, Flapping Eagle, a Native American, becomes immortal by drinking a magical liquid and wanders for 777 years, 7 months and 7 days before arriving on Calf Island.

**Other later works**
The Golden House (2017) follows Nero Golden, a man from Bombay who moves with his three sons to "the Gardens" in Greenwich Village. Quichotte (2019) is a modern American Don Quixote created inside the novel by the spy writer Sam DuChamp, and the hero imagines a black-and-white son. Shalimar the Clown (2005) involves the American ambassador Maximilian Ophuls and the Kashmiri dancer Boonyi, The Enchantress of Florence (2008) is partly set at the court of Akbar the Great, and the story collection East, West includes "Chekov and Zulu."
